Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A,P)$ be a probability space, let $n\ge1$ be an integer, and let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_n$ be IID random elements with law $P$. For a class $\mathcal F$ of measurable, integrable real-valued functions on $\mathcal X$, write

$$Pf:=\int f\,dP,\qquad P_nf:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n f(Z_i),\qquad \mathbb G_n(f):=\sqrt n\,(P_nf-Pf).$$

The map $f\mapsto P_nf-Pf$ is the centered empirical process, and $\mathbb G_n$ is its $\sqrt n$-scaled version. More generally, for independent processes $X_1(t),\ldots,X_n(t)$ whose marginal expectations are finite for each index $t\in T$, the centered process sum is

$$S_n(t):=\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl(X_i(t)-\mathbb E X_i(t)\bigr),\qquad t\in T.$$

On an auxiliary probability-space extension, let $\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_n$ be independent signs, each taking $+1$ and $-1$ with probability $1/2$, independent of the observations. The empirical Rademacher process is

$$R_n(f):=\sum_{i=1}^n\sigma_i f(Z_i),\qquad f\in\mathcal F.$$

The centered Rademacher process $\sum_i\sigma_i(f(Z_i)-Pf)$ is a distinct process; no equality between it and $R_n$ is part of this definition.

For a countable class of measurable functions, each displayed supremum of measurable sample paths is measurable. For an uncountable class, ordinary probability or expectation is used only when a specified countable subclass has the same supremum almost surely for the process in question; this is the separable-version convention used here. Otherwise state results using outer probability

$$P^*(A):=\inf\{P(B):A\subseteq B,\ B\in\mathcal A\}$$

and, for a nonnegative possibly nonmeasurable random quantity $Y$, outer expectation

$$\mathbb E^*Y:=\inf\{\mathbb E U: U\text{ is measurable, nonnegative, and }U\ge Y\}.$$

In particular, measurability of every $f$ separately does not by itself make an uncountable supremum measurable.

A pseudometric $d$ on a set $T$ is a nonnegative symmetric function $d:T\times T\to[0,\infty)$ with $d(t,t)=0$ and $d(s,t)\le d(s,u)+d(u,t)$; distinct points may have distance zero. For a nonempty subset $\mathcal F\subseteq T$ and $\epsilon>0$, the covering number $N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ is the least finite $k$ for which there are centers $f_1,\ldots,f_k\in\mathcal F$ such that every $f\in\mathcal F$ satisfies $d(f,f_j)\le\epsilon$ for some $j$. It is $+\infty$ if no finite cover exists. Set $N(\epsilon,\varnothing,d)=1$.

The packing number $D(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ is the largest size of a finite subset $\{f_1,\ldots,f_k\}\subseteq\mathcal F$ whose distinct members have pairwise distance strictly greater than $\epsilon$. If the sizes of such finite subsets are unbounded, put $D=+\infty$; put $D(\epsilon,\varnothing,d)=0$. These conventions give the radius comparison proved in [[lem-packing-covering-number-comparison]]. The metric entropy is $H(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d):=\log N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ for nonempty classes, with $\log(+\infty)=+\infty$.

For a probability measure $Q$ on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ and a measurable real function $g$, set $\|g\|_{Q,r}:=(\int |g|^r\,dQ)^{1/r}$ for $1\le r<\infty$, using the positive-base real-power convention of [[def-real-power]]. The function $|g|$ is measurable by [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]], and [[lem-real-power-preserves-measurability]] makes $|g|^r$ measurable, so this integral is well-defined. On a class of functions with finite such norms, $d_{Q,r}(f,g):=\|f-g\|_{Q,r}$ is a pseudometric: nonnegativity, symmetry, and zero diagonal follow from the absolute value, and the triangle inequality is [[thm-minkowski-inequality-for-integrals]]. Functions that agree $Q$-almost everywhere have distance zero. We write $N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,L^r(Q))$ for this covering number.

For measurable real endpoints $\ell\le u$ $Q$-almost everywhere, the bracket $[\ell,u]$ is the set of measurable functions $f$ satisfying $\ell\le f\le u$ $Q$-almost everywhere. Its $L^r(Q)$ width is $\|u-\ell\|_{Q,r}$. The bracketing number $N_{[]} (\epsilon,\mathcal F,L^r(Q))$ is the least number of such brackets of width at most $\epsilon$ that cover $\mathcal F$, or $+\infty$ if no finite cover exists; for the empty class set it equal to $1$. Centers of metric covers are in $\mathcal F$; bracket endpoints need not be.

Use the real random variable convention of [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]] and the expectation convention of [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. A real random variable $X$ is **centered** when it is integrable and $\mathbb E X=0$. A vector random element $Z=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_d)$ in $\mathbb R^d$, for an integer $d\ge1$, is centered when each coordinate is integrable and $\mathbb E Z_j=0$. For $u,z\in\mathbb R^d$, write $\langle u,z\rangle=\sum_{j=1}^d u_jz_j$ and $\|u\|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^d u_j^2)^{1/2}$, using the Euclidean convention in [[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]].

For $\sigma^2\ge0$, a centered real random variable $X$ is **sub-Gaussian with proxy $\sigma^2$** if
$$\mathbb E e^{\lambda X}\le e^{\lambda^2\sigma^2/2}\qquad\text{for every }\lambda\in\mathbb R.$$
A centered vector random element $Z\in\mathbb R^d$ is **sub-Gaussian with proxy $\sigma^2$** if
$$\mathbb E e^{\lambda\langle u,Z\rangle}\le e^{\sigma^2\lambda^2\|u\|_2^2/2}\qquad\text{for every }u\in\mathbb R^d\text{ and }\lambda\in\mathbb R.$$

For $\nu^2\ge0$ and $b>0$, a centered real random variable $X$ is **sub-exponential with parameters $(\nu^2,b)$** if
$$\mathbb E e^{\lambda X}\le e^{\lambda^2\nu^2/2}\qquad\text{whenever }|\lambda|\le1/b.$$

The parameters $\sigma^2$ and $\nu^2$ are moment-generating-function upper-bound proxies; they are not asserted to equal the variance. The vector condition controls every one-dimensional projection and does not assert independence of coordinates.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $X$ be an
integrable real random variable, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval
containing $X(\omega)$ for almost every $\omega$, and let $\varphi:I\to\mathbb R$
be convex.

Assume additionally that $\varphi(X)$ is either integrable or nonnegative, so
its expectation is defined by
[[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Then
$$\varphi(\mathbb E[X])\le\mathbb E[\varphi(X)].$$
In the nonnegative case the right-hand side may be $+\infty$.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

Let $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$ be measurable and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $A,B\in\mathcal F$,
and let $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be events.

1. $\mathbb P(A^c)=1-\mathbb P(A)$.
2. If $A\subseteq B$, then $\mathbb P(A)\le\mathbb P(B)$.
3. If $A\subseteq B$, then $\mathbb P(B\setminus A)=\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A)$.
4. $\mathbb P(\bigcup_n A_n)\le\sum_{n=0}^\infty \mathbb P(A_n)$, and for every
   natural $m$,
   $$\mathbb P\left(\bigcup_{n<m}A_n\right)\le\sum_{n<m}\mathbb P(A_n).$$
5. $\mathbb P(A\cup B)=\mathbb P(A)+\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A\cap B)$.
6. If $A_n\uparrow A$, then
   $$\mathbb P(A)=\sup_n\mathbb P(A_n).$$
   If $A_n\downarrow A$, then
   $$\mathbb P(A)=\inf_n\mathbb P(A_n).$$

Since the specified countable dense set is listed, choose the first finite tuple under its induced enumeration that is an $\epsilon_k$-net and has cardinality at most this cover size; such a tuple exists by the construction. Denote it by $T_k$. For each $t$, choose the least-index point $\pi_k(t)\in T_k$ within $\epsilon_k$. These canonical choices across scales require no choice axiom. Put $T_0^{(0)}=\{t_0\}$ and $\pi_0(t)=t_0$.

For a finite subset $A\subset T_0$, telescope $X_t-X_{t_0}$ through $\pi_1(t),\ldots,\pi_m(t)$ for every $t\in A$. At level $1$ there are at most $|T_1|$ increments, each with proxy at most $D^2$; for $k\ge2$ there are at most $|T_k||T_{k-1}|$ increments, each with proxy at most $(\epsilon_k+\epsilon_{k-1})^2=(3\epsilon_k)^2$. Applying step 1.1 to the finite set of increments at each level, and the triangle inequality for their maxima, yields $\mathbb E\max_{t\in A}|X_{\pi_m(t)}-X_{t_0}|\le C_1\sum_{k=1}^m\epsilon_k\sqrt{1+\log N(\epsilon_k/4,T,d)}$ for a universal $C_1$; the $k=1$ term is absorbed using $\epsilon_1=D/2$ and $N(\epsilon_1/4)\ge1$.

The residual maximum over $A$ has expectation at most $\epsilon_m\sqrt{2\log(2|A|)}$ by step 1.1, since $d(t,\pi_m(t))\le\epsilon_m$. Letting $m\to\infty$ for this fixed finite $A$ removes the residual. The dyadic sum in step 2.2 is bounded by a universal multiple of the entropy integral: on each interval $[\epsilon_k/8,\epsilon_k/4]$, monotonicity of $N$ makes the integral at least $(\epsilon_k/8)\sqrt{\log N(\epsilon_k/4,T,d)}$. Also, for $0<\epsilon<D/2$, one ball of radius $\epsilon$ cannot cover a set of diameter $D$, so $N(\epsilon,T,d)\ge2$ and the entropy integral is at least $(D/2)\sqrt{\log2}$; this absorbs the geometric contribution from the added $1$. Hence $\mathbb E\max_{t\in A}|X_t-X_{t_0}|\le C\int_0^D\sqrt{\log N(\epsilon,T,d)}\,d\epsilon.$ Taking an increasing sequence of finite subsets whose union is $T_0$, [F5] and the separability assumption give the asserted supremum over $T$.

By [F7], $P\Delta_qg\to0$; by [F5] and the integrable majorant $2H$, the pointwise limit of $\Delta_qg$ consequently has integral zero and is zero $P$-almost everywhere. Countability of $\mathcal G$ and finiteness of each partition give one common full-measure set on which all envelope and oscillation bounds hold and every oscillation tends to zero; iid observations avoid its null complement almost surely. Define $A_qg=\prod_{p=q_0}^q\mathbf1_{\{\Delta_pg\le\sqrt n a_p\}},\quad B_{q_0}g=\mathbf1_{\{\Delta_{q_0}g>\sqrt n a_{q_0}\}},\quad B_qg=A_{q-1}g\mathbf1_{\{\Delta_qg>\sqrt n a_q\}}\ (q>q_0).$ Nestedness makes these indicators constant on the corresponding cells. At each point either every cutoff passes or there is a unique first failed cutoff. In the first case, $\pi_qg\to g$ by the vanishing oscillation; in the second, the sum stops at that first failure. In either case, pointwise telescoping gives $g-\pi_{q_0}g=(g-\pi_{q_0}g)B_{q_0}g+\sum_{q>q_0}(g-\pi_qg)B_qg+\sum_{q>q_0}(\pi_qg-\pi_{q-1}g)A_{q-1}g.$

The $m_{q_0}$ representatives $\pi_{q_0}(C)$ have $L^2(P)$ norm at most $M_{\mathcal G}$. Clip each representative to zero on $\{H>\sqrt n a_{q_0}\}$. Since $m_{q_0+1}\ge m_{q_0}$, the definition of $a_{q_0}$ absorbs the second term into $2^{-q_0}\|H\|_{P,2}\sqrt{L_{q_0}}$. Thus the coarse representatives contribute at most the first and tail terms in the claimed bound, up to a universal factor.

The first term on the right of step 1.2 is bounded by $2H\mathbf1_{\{H>\sqrt n a_{q_0}/2\}}$, because $\Delta_{q_0}g>\sqrt n a_{q_0}$ and $\Delta_{q_0}g\le2H$. The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most

derivations.claim: Choose a countable pointwise-dense subclass $\mathcal F_0\subseteq\mathcal F$. For $\delta>0$, set $\mathcal H_\delta=\{(f-g)-P(f-g):f,g\in\mathcal F_0,\ \rho_P(f,g)\le\delta\}$. Every $h\in\mathcal H_\delta$ has $\|h\|_{P,2}\le\delta$ and is bounded in absolute value by $H:=2F+2PF$, with $\|H\|_{P,2}\le4\|F\|_{P,2}$.

If $f$ and $g$ lie in $L^2(P)$ brackets $[l_i,u_i]$ and $[l_j,u_j]$ of width at most $r\|F\|_{P,2}$, respectively, then $(f-g)-P(f-g)$ lies in the bracket $[l_i-u_j-P(u_i-l_j),\ u_i-l_j-P(l_i-u_j)].$ Its width is $w_i+w_j+P(w_i+w_j)$, where $w_i=u_i-l_i$ and $w_j=u_j-l_j$; Cauchy–Schwarz gives its $L^2(P)$ norm at most $2(\|w_i\|_{P,2}+\|w_j\|_{P,2})\le4r\|F\|_{P,2}$. If $b_q$ is the unrefined level-$q$ count, step 1.2 gives $b_q\le N_{[]} (r_q\|F\|_{P,2},\mathcal F,L^2(P))^2$ for $r_q=2^{-q}\|H\|_{P,2}/(4\|F\|_{P,2})$, and the refined count satisfies $m_q\le\prod_{p=q_0}^q b_p$. Let $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A,P)$ be a probability space, let $n\ge1$ be an integer, and let $Z_1,\ldots,Z_n$ be IID random elements with law $P$. For a class $\mathcal F$ of measurable, integrable real-valued functions on $\mathcal X$, write

$$Pf:=\int f\,dP,\qquad P_nf:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n f(Z_i),\qquad \mathbb G_n(f):=\sqrt n\,(P_nf-Pf).$$

The map $f\mapsto P_nf-Pf$ is the centered empirical process, and $\mathbb G_n$ is its $\sqrt n$-scaled version. More generally, for independent processes $X_1(t),\ldots,X_n(t)$ whose marginal expectations are finite for each index $t\in T$, the centered process sum is

$$S_n(t):=\sum_{i=1}^n\bigl(X_i(t)-\mathbb E X_i(t)\bigr),\qquad t\in T.$$

On an auxiliary probability-space extension, let $\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_n$ be independent signs, each taking $+1$ and $-1$ with probability $1/2$, independent of the observations. The empirical Rademacher process is

$$R_n(f):=\sum_{i=1}^n\sigma_i f(Z_i),\qquad f\in\mathcal F.$$

The centered Rademacher process $\sum_i\sigma_i(f(Z_i)-Pf)$ is a distinct process; no equality between it and $R_n$ is part of this definition.

For a countable class of measurable functions, each displayed supremum of measurable sample paths is measurable. For an uncountable class, ordinary probability or expectation is used only when a specified countable subclass has the same supremum almost surely for the process in question; this is the separable-version convention used here. Otherwise state results using outer probability

$$P^*(A):=\inf\{P(B):A\subseteq B,\ B\in\mathcal A\}$$

and, for a nonnegative possibly nonmeasurable random quantity $Y$, outer expectation

$$\mathbb E^*Y:=\inf\{\mathbb E U: U\text{ is measurable, nonnegative, and }U\ge Y\}.$$

In particular, measurability of every $f$ separately does not by itself make an uncountable supremum measurable.

A pseudometric $d$ on a set $T$ is a nonnegative symmetric function $d:T\times T\to[0,\infty)$ with $d(t,t)=0$ and $d(s,t)\le d(s,u)+d(u,t)$; distinct points may have distance zero. For a nonempty subset $\mathcal F\subseteq T$ and $\epsilon>0$, the covering number $N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ is the least finite $k$ for which there are centers $f_1,\ldots,f_k\in\mathcal F$ such that every $f\in\mathcal F$ satisfies $d(f,f_j)\le\epsilon$ for some $j$. It is $+\infty$ if no finite cover exists. Set $N(\epsilon,\varnothing,d)=1$.

The packing number $D(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ is the largest size of a finite subset $\{f_1,\ldots,f_k\}\subseteq\mathcal F$ whose distinct members have pairwise distance strictly greater than $\epsilon$. If the sizes of such finite subsets are unbounded, put $D=+\infty$; put $D(\epsilon,\varnothing,d)=0$. These conventions give the radius comparison proved in [[lem-packing-covering-number-comparison]]. The metric entropy is $H(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d):=\log N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ for nonempty classes, with $\log(+\infty)=+\infty$.

For a probability measure $Q$ on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ and a measurable real function $g$, set $\|g\|_{Q,r}:=(\int |g|^r\,dQ)^{1/r}$ for $1\le r<\infty$, using the positive-base real-power convention of [[def-real-power]]. The function $|g|$ is measurable by [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]], and [[lem-real-power-preserves-measurability]] makes $|g|^r$ measurable, so this integral is well-defined. On a class of functions with finite such norms, $d_{Q,r}(f,g):=\|f-g\|_{Q,r}$ is a pseudometric: nonnegativity, symmetry, and zero diagonal follow from the absolute value, and the triangle inequality is [[thm-minkowski-inequality-for-integrals]]. Functions that agree $Q$-almost everywhere have distance zero. We write $N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,L^r(Q))$ for this covering number.

For measurable real endpoints $\ell\le u$ $Q$-almost everywhere, the bracket $[\ell,u]$ is the set of measurable functions $f$ satisfying $\ell\le f\le u$ $Q$-almost everywhere. Its $L^r(Q)$ width is $\|u-\ell\|_{Q,r}$. The bracketing number $N_{[]} (\epsilon,\mathcal F,L^r(Q))$ is the least number of such brackets of width at most $\epsilon$ that cover $\mathcal F$, or $+\infty$ if no finite cover exists; for the empty class set it equal to $1$. Centers of metric covers are in $\mathcal F$; bracket endpoints need not be.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Let $d\ge1$ be fixed. Let $Z_n$ be random elements of the finite-dimensional Euclidean space $\mathbb R^d$, not necessarily defined on a common probability space, and let $
u$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^d$. The sequence $(Z_n)$ has **asymptotic distribution** $
u$ if its laws converge weakly to $
u$; equivalently, $Z_n\Rightarrow Z$ for any random vector $Z$ with law $
u$ ([[def-convergence-in-distribution-of-random-elements]], [[def-weak-convergence-of-borel-probability-measures]]).

For an estimator, any centering or scaling, such as $r_n(T_n-\psi(	heta))$, is part of the sequence whose asymptotic distribution is being specified; it is not implicit in the term. Weak convergence alone does not assert convergence of moments.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer. Let $(X_k)_{k\ge1}$ be iid $\mathbb R^d$-valued random vectors with $\mathbb E\|X_1\|^2<\infty$, mean m and covariance Sigma. Then $$n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=1}^n(X_k-m)\Rightarrow N_d(0,\Sigma).$$ The covariance may be singular.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For any set $I$, standard-Borel coordinate spaces $(E_i,\mathcal E_i)$, and consistent finite-dimensional laws $(\mu_F)_{F\Subset I}$, there is a unique probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathcal C_I$ whose $F$-coordinate marginal is $\mu_F$ for each finite $F$.

Let $(T,d)$ be a nonempty pseudometric space that is totally bounded in the following sense: for every $r>0$ there is a finite set $E_r\subseteq T$ such that $T\subseteq\bigcup_{e\in E_r}\{t\in T:d(t,e)\le r\}$. Its diameter is $D:=\sup_{s,t\in T}d(s,t)<\infty$. For each $t\in T$, let $X_t$ be a real random variable. Assume the process is separable: a specified countable dense subset $T_0\subseteq T$, equipped with a fixed listing, has the property that the supremum of every process increment over $T$ equals its supremum over $T_0$ almost surely. Suppose all increments are centered and sub-Gaussian with their $d$-scale, meaning that for every $s,t\in T$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb R$,

$$\mathbb E\exp\{\lambda(X_s-X_t)\}\le\exp\{\lambda^2d(s,t)^2/2\}.$$

If

$$\int_0^D\sqrt{\log N(\epsilon,T,d)}\,d\epsilon<\infty,$$

where $N(\epsilon,T,d)$ is the least number of closed $d$-balls of radius $\epsilon$ covering $T$ ([[def-covering-packing-bracketing-number-and-metric-entropy]]), then for every $t_0\in T$,

$$\mathbb E\sup_{t\in T}|X_t-X_{t_0}|\le C\int_0^D\sqrt{\log N(\epsilon,T,d)}\,d\epsilon$$

for a universal constant $C$. If $D=0$, the integral and the supremum are both zero.

For a class $\mathcal H$ of measurable real functions under a probability measure $Q$, an **envelope** $H$ means a nonnegative measurable function with $|h|\le H$ $Q$-almost surely for every $h\in\mathcal H$. Cauchy–Schwarz [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]] gives $QH\le\|H\|_{Q,2}<\infty$ when $H\in L^2(Q)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be iid with law $P$, and let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty pointwise-measurable class of measurable functions with a nonnegative envelope $F$ satisfying $PF^2<\infty$. Assume $0<\|F\|_{P,2}<\infty$ and

$$\int_0^1\sqrt{\log N_{[]}\bigl(\epsilon\|F\|_{P,2},\mathcal F,L^2(P)\bigr)}\,d\epsilon<\infty.$$

Use the empirical process $\mathbb G_n$ and semimetric $\rho_P$ from [[def-empirical-process-and-rademacher-process]] and [[def-donsker-class-and-asymptotic-equicontinuity]]. Then $\mathbb G_n$ is asymptotically equicontinuous in probability with respect to $\rho_P$.

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice for assertion 5 and the consequent
existence claim ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space
([[def-metric-space]]) and let $\mathcal{C}$ be the set of all Cauchy sequences
in $X$ ([[def-cauchy-in-metric]]). Then:

1. For all $x = (x_n)$ and $y = (y_n)$ in $\mathcal{C}$ the real sequence
   $\big(d(x_n,y_n)\big)_n$ converges, so
   $$\rho(x,y) \;:=\; \lim_{n} d(x_n,y_n)$$
   is a single well-determined real ([[thm-cauchy-criterion-via-lub]],
   [[lem-limit-unique]]).
2. The relation $x \sim y :\Longleftrightarrow \rho(x,y) = 0$ is an equivalence
   relation on $\mathcal{C}$. Write $\widehat{X} := \mathcal{C}/\!\sim$ for the
   set of its classes and $[x]$ for the class of $x$.
3. $\widehat{d}\big([x],[y]\big) := \rho(x,y)$ does not depend on the chosen
   representatives, and $\widehat{d}$ is a metric on $\widehat{X}$.
4. The map $\iota : X \to \widehat{X}$ sending $p$ to the class of the constant
   sequence at $p$ is an isometric embedding with dense image
   ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]],
   [[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]).
5. $(\widehat{X}, \widehat{d})$ is complete.

Consequently $\big((\widehat{X},\widehat{d}), \iota\big)$ is a completion of
$(X,d)$ ([[def-metric-completion]]), and **every metric space has a
completion**.

**The notation is kept honest.** A Cauchy sequence in $X$ need not converge in
$X$, so no symbol $\lim_n x_n$ appears anywhere below; the only limits taken are
limits of *real* sequences, and each is written only after its existence has been
proved. The equivalence relation is defined and verified here rather than cited, as was
done for [[def-integers]], so that the construction is self-contained and its
transitivity argument is visible at the point of use.

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice** ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $(X,d)$
be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) that is complete
([[def-complete-metric-space]]) and totally bounded ([[def-totally-bounded]]).
Then $(X,d)$ is compact ([[def-metric-compactness]]).

**Where the axiom is spent, and why the weaker principle suffices.**
$\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is used exactly once, at step 3.1, to fix one finite
$1/(n+1)$-net **together with a listing of it** for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ at
once. The family of sets being chosen from is written down before any selection
is made and does not depend on the earlier selections, which is precisely the
situation countable choice covers and dependent choice
([[def-dependent-choice]]) is not needed for. Everything after step 3.1 is
canonical: at each stage the construction takes the **least** admissible index in
the listing already fixed.

As always on this page, the claim is an upper bound on the cost of the proof
given here, not an assertion that $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is necessary for the
theorem.

Let $(K,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space. Every member of
$C(K,\mathbb{R})$ is bounded, so the supremum metric

$$d_\infty(f,g):=\sup_{x\in K}|f(x)-g(x)|$$

is defined on $C(K,\mathbb{R})$. With this metric,
$C(K,\mathbb{R})$ is complete.
Assume AC. For a compact metric K, $C(K;\mathbb R)$ has a countable uniformly dense subset in the supremum norm.

A topological space is **Polish** when it is separable ([[def-separable-space]]) and completely metrizable: its topology is induced by some complete metric ([[lem-complete-remetrisation]]). No particular compatible complete metric or countable dense subset is part of the structure.
Assume AC. Every Borel probability on a Polish space S is tight.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

Let $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be events in a probability space. If
$$\sum_{n=0}^\infty \mathbb P(A_n)<+\infty,$$
then
$$\mathbb P(A_n\ \mathrm{i.o.})=0.$$

No independence hypothesis is needed.

Assume AC. If $X$ has law $N(m,\sigma^2)$ with $\sigma\ge0$, then $\varphi_X(t)=\exp(imt-\sigma^2t^2/2)$ for every real $t$. Moreover $\mathbb EX=m$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2$, including $\sigma=0$.

Assume AC. Two Borel probability laws on $\mathbb R$ with equal characteristic functions are equal. In particular a real random variable has a real-valued characteristic function if and only if its law is symmetric under $x\mapsto-x$.

1. $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$ with the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) is a complete metric space
   ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).
2. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on
   $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ is complete.

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited and is not decoration.**
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] defines $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its three metrics only for
$n \ge 1$, because at $n = 0$ the metric $d_\infty$ would be a maximum over the
empty index set. Every statement about $\mathbb{R}^n$ in this library carries the
hypothesis, and this one does too.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[def-real-numbers]]) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

A topological space is **Polish** when it is separable ([[def-separable-space]]) and completely metrizable: its topology is induced by some complete metric ([[lem-complete-remetrisation]]). No particular compatible complete metric or countable dense subset is part of the structure.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer and $p_\theta(x)=\theta\cdot x$ for $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$. Borel probability laws on $\mathbb R^d$ are determined by all the laws $(p_\theta)_*\mu$. Moreover, if $(p_\theta)_*\mu_n\Rightarrow(p_\theta)_*\mu$ for every $\theta$ and a specified Borel probability law $\mu$, then $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$. If dimension zero is admitted, interpret $\mathbb R^0$ as the singleton empty tuple; both conclusions then hold as well.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $A,B\in\mathcal F$,
and let $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be events.

1. $\mathbb P(A^c)=1-\mathbb P(A)$.
2. If $A\subseteq B$, then $\mathbb P(A)\le\mathbb P(B)$.
3. If $A\subseteq B$, then $\mathbb P(B\setminus A)=\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A)$.
4. $\mathbb P(\bigcup_n A_n)\le\sum_{n=0}^\infty \mathbb P(A_n)$, and for every
   natural $m$,
   $$\mathbb P\left(\bigcup_{n<m}A_n\right)\le\sum_{n<m}\mathbb P(A_n).$$
5. $\mathbb P(A\cup B)=\mathbb P(A)+\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A\cap B)$.
6. If $A_n\uparrow A$, then
   $$\mathbb P(A)=\sup_n\mathbb P(A_n).$$
   If $A_n\downarrow A$, then
   $$\mathbb P(A)=\inf_n\mathbb P(A_n).$$

derivations.claim: If $\|F\|_{P,2}=0$, every member of a countable pointwise-dense subclass is zero $P$-almost surely. By [F15], countable subadditivity gives a probability-one event on which all those functions vanish at every observation. Pointwise approximation then makes every $f\in\mathcal F$ vanish at the observations; dominated convergence gives $Pf=0$ for each $f$. Thus $\mathbb G_n$ is the zero process in outer probability and the conclusion holds with the zero Gaussian bridge.

Assume $\|F\|_{P,2}>0$. Each finite $L^2(P)$ bracket of width $r$ has $\rho_P$-diameter at most $r$, because $\rho_P(f,g)\le\|f-g\|_{P,2}\le\|u-l\|_{P,2}$. The entropy integral being finite forces $N_{[]}(r,\mathcal F,L^2(P))<\infty$ for every $r>0$: if it were infinite at one positive scale, monotonicity would make the integral infinite on an interval below that scale. Therefore the quotient of $\mathcal F$ by zero $\rho_P$-distance is totally bounded. The countable pointwise-dense subclass is dense in this quotient, since $|f_k-f|^2\le4F^2$ and [F7] gives $\|f_k-f\|_{P,2}\to0$.

Enumerate the countable dense subclass as $\mathcal F_0=\{f_j:j\in J\}$. For any finite list $f_{j_1},\ldots,f_{j_m}$, the covariance matrix $\Sigma_{ab}=K(f_{j_a},f_{j_b})$ is positive semidefinite, since $c^T\Sigma c=P[\sum_a c_a(f_{j_a}-Pf_{j_a})]^2\ge0$. [F3] supplies the centered Gaussian law $N_m(0,\Sigma)$. For any sublist, both the corresponding marginal and the Gaussian law constructed from its covariance have, in every direction, the same centered normal projection; [F14] makes the laws equal. Thus these finite-dimensional laws are consistent.

The coordinate space $\mathbb R$ with its Borel sigma-algebra is standard Borel by [F13], so [F4] extends the consistent Gaussian laws to a centered Gaussian process $\mathbb G_0$ indexed by $\mathcal F_0$, with covariance $K$. For $f,g\in\mathcal F_0$, its increment is centered normal with variance $\rho_P(f,g)^2$, hence its MGF is $\mathbb E e^{\lambda(\mathbb G_0(f)-\mathbb G_0(g))}=e^{\lambda^2\rho_P(f,g)^2/2}$.

For $\delta>0$, index the Gaussian increment process by pairs $(f,g)\in\mathcal F_0^2$ with $\rho_P(f,g)\le\delta$, and write $Y_{f,g}=\mathbb G_0(f)-\mathbb G_0(g)$. Its canonical pseudometric is $d_Y((f,g),(f',g'))=\{E[(Y_{f,g}-Y_{f',g'})^2]\}^{1/2}$. The triangle inequality in $L^2(P)$ gives $d_Y\le\rho_P(f,f')+\rho_P(g,g')$, while every $Y_{f,g}$ has standard deviation at most $\delta$, so the $d_Y$-diameter of this pair set is at most $2\delta$. A product of two $\epsilon/4$-nets of $\mathcal F_0$ covers the pair set within $d_Y$-distance $\epsilon/2$. Its centers might lie outside the restricted pair set; from each product ball that meets the pair set, choose one pair inside it. The triangle inequality then gives an $\epsilon$-net with centers in the pair set and cardinality at most $N(\epsilon/4,\mathcal F_0,\rho_P)^2$. Applying [F5] with the diagonal base point $(f_*,f_*)$ yields $E\sup_{f,g\in\mathcal F_0:\,\rho_P(f,g)\le\delta}|\mathbb G_0(f)-\mathbb G_0(g)|\le C\int_0^{C'\delta}\sqrt{\log N(\epsilon,\mathcal F_0,\rho_P)}\,d\epsilon,$ which tends to zero as $\delta\downarrow0$ by the bracketing cover bound in step 1.2.

Choose rational $\delta_k\downarrow0$ so that the expectation in step 3.1 is at most $2^{-3k}$. By [F11], the probability that the corresponding modulus exceeds $2^{-k}$ is at most $2^{-2k}$, and the first Borel–Cantelli lemma makes only finitely many such events occur almost surely. Thus the Gaussian sample paths are uniformly $\rho_P$-continuous on $\mathcal F_0$ almost surely. By [A2], Countable Choice is available for the metric-completion construction in [F8], so the metric quotient embeds densely in a complete metric completion $T$; compactness and the pathwise extension are established below.

Fix $\varepsilon>0$ and take a finite $\varepsilon/2$-net in the totally bounded metric quotient from step 1.2. Its image in $T$ is still a finite $\varepsilon/2$-net for the dense embedded quotient. For any $x\in T$, density gives a quotient point $q$ with $d(x,q)<\varepsilon/2$, and some net point $y$ satisfies $d(q,y)\le\varepsilon/2$; hence $d(x,y)<\varepsilon$. Thus $T$ is totally bounded, and it is compact by its completeness from [F8] and the complete-plus-totally-bounded theorem in [F8]. To extend a path $G_0$ that is uniformly $\rho_P$-continuous on the listed dense subset $\mathcal F_0$, for each $x\in T$ and $n\ge1$ let $f_n(x)$ be the first listed point of $\mathcal F_0$ within $1/n$ of $x$. The sequence $G_0(f_n(x))$ is Cauchy by uniform continuity and therefore has a real limit by [F13]. Any two sequences from $\mathcal F_0$ converging to $x$ have pairwise distances tending to zero, so uniform continuity makes their value limits equal. Define $\overline G_0(x)$ by this common limit. To verify continuity, given $\eta>0$ choose $\tau>0$ so that $d(u,v)<\tau$ for $u,v\in\mathcal F_0$ implies $|G_0(u)-G_0(v)|<\eta/2$. If $d(x,y)<\tau/3$, approximating sequences $u_n\to x$ and $v_n\to y$ eventually satisfy $d(u_n,v_n)<\tau$; passing to their value limits gives $|\overline G_0(x)-\overline G_0(y)|\le\eta/2<\eta$. Density makes this extension unique.

Uniform continuity on the countable set $\mathcal F_0$ is a measurable path event: for each integer $m$, the condition that some positive rational radius makes every coordinate increment below $1/m$ for pairs in $\mathcal F_0$ closer than that radius is a countable union and intersection of measurable coordinate events. By step 4.1 this event has probability one. On it use the extension from step 4.2, and define the function to be zero off it. The resulting map is a Borel random element of $C(T,\mathbb R)$: evaluations at the countable dense set $\mathcal F_0$ are measurable, and for continuous functions the supremum distance is the supremum over $\mathcal F_0$, so preimages of open balls are measurable; separability makes every open set a countable union of such balls. By [F9], $C(T,\mathbb R)$ is complete and separable; [F10] makes it Polish and its Gaussian law tight. For each $f\in\mathcal F$, choose pointwise approximants $f_k\in\mathcal F_0$. By [F7], $\|f_k-f\|_{P,2}\to0$, so the corresponding Gaussian coordinates converge in $L^2$. For any finite list $f_1,\ldots,f_m$ and coefficients $c_1,\ldots,c_m$, the approximating linear combinations are centered normal with variances $\sigma_k^2$ converging to $\sigma^2=\sum_{i,j}c_ic_jK(f_i,f_j)=P[\sum_i c_i(f_i-Pf_i)]^2\ge0$. Their $L^2$ convergence implies convergence of characteristic functions, because $|e^{itx}-e^{ity}|\le|t||x-y|$. By [F12], the limit characteristic function is $e^{-t^2\sigma^2/2}$ and determines the centered normal law of variance $\sigma^2$. Every linear combination of the limiting vector is therefore centered normal; [F3] identifies that vector as multivariate normal with covariance $(K(f_i,f_j))$. The pathwise extension from step 4.1 is the same limit in probability, so uniqueness of probability limits identifies its coordinates with these Gaussian limits. Define $R:C(T,\mathbb R)\to\ell^\infty(\mathcal F)$ by $R(z)(f)=z([f])$, where $[f]$ is the image of $f$ in the metric quotient and its completion. Since these images are dense in $T$ and $z-w$ is continuous, $\|R(z)-R(w)\|_{\mathcal F}=\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}|z([f])-w([f])|=\sup_{t\in T}|z(t)-w(t)|$, so $R$ is an isometry and is continuous. Its pushforward of the tight Borel law on $C(T,\mathbb R)$ is a tight Borel Gaussian bridge on $\ell^\infty(\mathcal F)$.

Fix any finite $f_1,\ldots,f_m\in\mathcal F$. The vectors $(f_1(X_i)-Pf_1,\ldots,f_m(X_i)-Pf_m)$ are iid and have finite second moments, bounded in squared norm by a constant times $F(X_i)^2$. [F2] gives convergence of their normalized sums to $N_m(0,(K(f_a,f_b))_{a,b})$, the corresponding finite-dimensional law of the Gaussian bridge from step 5.1. This proves finite-dimensional convergence, with the asymptotic-distribution convention of [F1].

By [F6], the empirical processes are asymptotically equicontinuous in $\rho_P$. For each $\epsilon>0$, the totally bounded quotient from step 1.2 has a finite $\epsilon/2$-net with centers in the dense subset $\mathcal F_0$; density then makes it an $\epsilon$-net for all of $\mathcal F$. List its finitely many centers and assign to each $f$ the first center within distance $\epsilon$, obtaining $\pi_\epsilon(f)$. Define $\mathbb G_{n,\epsilon}(f)=\mathbb G_n(\pi_\epsilon(f))$ and $\mathbb G_{\epsilon}(f)=\mathbb G_P(\pi_\epsilon(f))$. Their ranges lie in a finite-dimensional subspace of $\ell^\infty(\mathcal F)$; the linear map from the selected coordinate vector to that subspace is continuous in the supremum norm. Thus the finite-dimensional convergence in step 6.1, tested after composition with any bounded continuous functional, gives $\mathbb G_{n,\epsilon}\Rightarrow\mathbb G_\epsilon$ for each fixed $\epsilon$.

The sup-norm error $\|\mathbb G_n-\mathbb G_{n,\epsilon}\|_{\mathcal F}$ is bounded by the empirical-process modulus over pairs at $\rho_P$-distance at most $\epsilon$; it is therefore bounded by the modulus at radius $2\epsilon$ in [F6], which tends to zero in outer probability as $\epsilon\downarrow0$. For measurable real endpoints $\ell\le u$ $Q$-almost everywhere, the bracket $[\ell,u]$ is the set of measurable functions $f$ satisfying $\ell\le f\le u$ $Q$-almost everywhere. Its $L^r(Q)$ width is $\|u-\ell\|_{Q,r}$. The bracketing number $N_{[]} (\epsilon,\mathcal F,L^r(Q))$ is the least number of such brackets of width at most $\epsilon$ that cover $\mathcal F$, or $+\infty$ if no finite cover exists; for the empty class set it equal to $1$. Centers of metric covers are in $\mathcal F$; bracket endpoints need not be.

For a class $\mathcal H$ of measurable real functions under a probability measure $Q$, an **envelope** $H$ means a nonnegative measurable function with $|h|\le H$ $Q$-almost surely for every $h\in\mathcal H$. Cauchy–Schwarz [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]] gives $QH\le\|H\|_{Q,2}<\infty$ when $H\in L^2(Q)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be iid with law $P$ on a measurable space, and let $\mathcal F$ be a nonempty pointwise-measurable class of measurable real functions with a measurable envelope $F\ge0$ satisfying $PF^2<\infty$. If $\|F\|_{P,2}=0$, the empirical process is the zero process almost surely. Otherwise assume

$$\int_0^1\sqrt{\log N_{[]}\bigl(\epsilon\|F\|_{P,2},\mathcal F,L^2(P)\bigr)}\,d\epsilon<\infty,$$

where $N_{[]}(r,\mathcal F,L^2(P))$ is the least number of measurable brackets $[l,u]$ with $l\le f\le u$ $P$-almost surely and $\|u-l\|_{P,2}\le r$ that cover $\mathcal F$. Then $\mathcal F$ is $P$-Donsker in the sense of [[def-donsker-class-and-asymptotic-equicontinuity]]: the empirical process $\mathbb G_n=\sqrt n(P_n-P)$ converges weakly in outer expectation in $\ell^\infty(\mathcal F)$ to a tight centered Gaussian bridge with covariance

$$K(f,g)=P[(f-Pf)(g-Pg)].$$

The $L^2(P)$ bracketing number and width use [[def-covering-packing-bracketing-number-and-metric-entropy]].

derivations.claim: The class $\mathcal F=\{f_t:t\in[0,1]\}$ is pointwise measurable. Since $1\in\mathbb Q$, the rational thresholds together with $1$ are indexed by $\mathbb Q\cap[0,1]$, which is countable by [F5]–[F6]. For each fixed $t<1$, [A2] and [F7] give rationals $q_k\in\mathbb Q\cap(t,\min(1,t+1/k))$, so $q_k\to t$ from above and $f_{q_k}(x)\to f_t(x)$ for every $x\in[0,1]$. The envelope $F\equiv1$ is measurable and square-integrable.

For an integer $m\ge1$, the $m$ brackets $[f_{j/m},f_{(j+1)/m}]$ have $L^2(P)$ width $\sqrt{1/m}$, since their endpoint difference is the indicator of an interval of length $1/m$. Thus for $0<\epsilon\le1$, choosing $m=\lceil\epsilon^{-2}\rceil$ gives $N_{[]} (\epsilon,\mathcal F,L^2(P))\le m$.

Consequently $\log N_{[]} (\epsilon,\mathcal F,L^2(P))\le\log(1+\epsilon^{-2})\le\log2+2\log(1/\epsilon)$ for $0<\epsilon\le1$. Since $\log(1/\epsilon)\le1/\epsilon$, the square-root entropy is bounded by $\sqrt{\log2}+\sqrt2\epsilon^{-1/2}$, an integrable function on $(0,1]$. All hypotheses of [F4] hold.

Applying [F4] gives a tight centered Gaussian limit. For $s,t\in[0,1]$, $P(f_sf_t)=P([0,\min(s,t)])=\min(s,t)$ and $Pf_sPf_t=st$, so [F2] gives covariance $\min(s,t)-st$. This is precisely the defining covariance of the standard Brownian bridge stated in the example, proving the claimed limit. AC is carried from [F4].
